_doc: T-0839. ONE PERSON, SEVERAL CARDS: the written ruling on every cluster of town cards that a surname-plus-compatible-forename test joins. The owner, 2026-09-05, reading the households folder: 'do a review and consolidate of the residents, like James Allen is almost certainly one record and he is spread across several, don't lose any data, but consolidation is needed across the residents' — and, when the first draft of this ticket stopped at a report, 'make the ticket merge those records — research without consolidation is useless'. This file is the RULING; tools/consolidate_town_cards.py derives the candidate clusters from the committed cards, refuses to pass its gate while any card in a candidate cluster carries no ruling here, and lands the merges. A ruling is a claim and carries its reasoning: `for` is the evidence the two cards name one person, `against` is what would say otherwise, and both are written even where the answer is obvious, because the next pass reads this instead of re-asking.

rules.C0: THE OWNER RULED IT. T-0839 names Allen, Hubbard, Owen, Fullerton, Kimberly and Haddock as merges in the ticket body: 'where the evidence is one man with a title, an initial and a full name, it is a MERGE'. This pass does not re-litigate them.
rules.C1: THE SAME NAME, TWICE. Two cards whose forenames are the same word or an unambiguous expansion of it, on the same source and the same date. Nothing distinguishes them at all.
rules.C2: AN INITIAL ONTO ITS ONE FULL FORENAME. The abbreviated card's initials agree letter for letter with the full-name card's, no middle initial contradicts, and exactly ONE full forename in the cluster carries the initial. Two rivals is a refusal, not a coin toss — the rule the newspapers' identity.json already ratified.
rules.C3: A BARE FORENAME ONTO AN ANCHOR. One card names a person the town DOCUMENTS — a trade, an arrival, a dwelling, a source that is not a bare list — and the other prints the same forename and surname with nothing that contradicts it, and the anchor is the only bearer of that forename in the cluster.
rules.C4: A CONTRADICTED MIDDLE INITIAL, OVER AN ANCHOR. The cluster holds one documented bearer of the forename, at least one card carries his full name, and the variation is confined to the middle initial across manuscript lists that a copyist mis-set. This is the rule the owner applied to Haddock (E / E. W. / Edward E. / Edward H.) and it is applied no further than that shape.
rules.R1: SURNAME AND A TITLE IS NOT A NAME. A card that prints no forename cannot be attached to one — the refusal data/research/newspapers/identity.json has ratified since the press pass.
rules.R2: TWO RIVALS IS A REFUSAL. An initial that could expand to two full forenames in the same cluster attaches to neither.
rules.R3: A CONTRADICTED MIDDLE INITIAL, WITH NO ANCHOR. Neither card documents the person beyond a list, and the two printed middle initials disagree. Either two men or one man mis-set, and nothing reached decides which.
rules.R4: A BARE FORENAME WITH NO ANCHOR. Neither card documents the person, so there is nothing for the bare forename to attach to. T-0696 is the ticket that would give this test a second discriminator.
rules.R5: A GARBLED FORENAME CANNOT BE TESTED. T-0695 is the ticket that reads them.
rules.D1: TWO PEOPLE THE SOURCES NAME SEPARATELY. A spouse, a sibling, a parent and child, or two explicit and different forenames.
rules.D2: A DATE CONTRADICTION. One card's person is dead, or absent, on a day the other's is documented alive in the town.
rules.C5: THE TRANSCRIBER NAMED HIM, IN BRACKETS. A reading that carries a bracketed forename — 'Hubbard, [Henry] G.' — is an editorial expansion by whoever transcribed the source: somebody looked at the page and said who this is. That names the person directly, so it outranks any inference drawn from the initials, and in particular it settles a cluster C2 would REFUSE for having two rivals. The bracket is evidence about identity; the initial is only evidence about spelling. Applied no further than a forename the transcription itself supplies.
rules.U1: UNDECIDED, AND THE QUESTION IS FILED. Two cards a candidate test joins where the answer needs a reading of the page rather than a rule — both readings are stated, neither is taken, and a ticket owns it. An undecided cluster still satisfies the gate, because the gate asks that a cluster be WEIGHED, not that it be merged.
rules.D3: A FEMALE HONORIFIC ON A MAN'S OWN NAME. `Mrs Rufus Brown` is not Rufus Brown. The honorific is stripped before two names are compared, which leaves the husband's forename tokens standing on both readings and makes the pair identical; a woman whose only printed name is her husband's is a real and common shape in this corpus and she is never her husband. The refusal is the card-side statement of R6 in tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py, which holds the two identities apart in the derivation, and it fires on the same evidence: a SOURCE that prints both readings as separate entries (T-0723).
rules.D4: THE CARDS STAY TWO BECAUSE NOTHING JOINS THEM. Two printings of one surname whose middle initials disagree, where C4 cannot fire — either no anchor exists, or the anchor's own record cannot reach the other card's date. This is NOT a claim that the town held two men of the name: it is the ruling that nothing reached folds them, and the record is carried as it is printed, which is the state the cards are already in. `for_merge` is kept verbatim so the argument survives its refusal and a later anchor can reopen it. R3 named this shape and referred it to the owner; T-0844 rules it instead, because a ballot between two guesses on no evidence is not a decision the owner is better placed to make than the rule is, and tickets/README.md holds `blocked-owner` to rights, licensing, money and what the project is.
rules.C6: A MIDDLE INITIAL STANDING ALONE, OVER AN ANCHOR THE SAME SOURCE PRINTS WITH BOTH INITIALS. All four of: the lone token is a forename initial for NO bearer in the cluster; exactly one documented bearer of the surname carries it as a middle initial; the same source prints that man with both initials, so the loss the fold supposes is one the source itself demonstrates; and the printing the folded card was minted from is flagged uncertain by its own extraction. Written for T-0844's Temple row and deliberately too narrow to reach a stray middle initial anywhere else — drop any one of the four conditions and the card stays where it is. This is the rule T-0839 declined to invent, written with the guard it wanted.
rules.C7: ONE COMPOUND SURNAME, PRINTED SEVERAL WAYS, RULED AT THE PAGE. Two cards whose surnames differ only in a Dutch, French or German particle — Van Den against Van der, De against Du — where all four of: the forename initial agrees on every printing; the SAME publication is shown setting the particle more than one way for that initial and stem inside the window, so the variation is demonstrated rather than supposed; the whole corpus holds exactly ONE bearer of the stem at this town; and no source places two such people here at once. The demonstration is the load-bearing clause and it is what separates C7 from a resemblance: a merge across two printed surnames needs the printer's own inconsistency in evidence, not the reader's willingness to believe in it. Written for T-0842, whose ticket says the same thing in its own words — 'a merge across two printed surnames is a research ruling and needs a source, not a resemblance'.
rules.C8: A MIDDLE NAME IN FULL, STANDING ALONE, WHERE A SOURCE PRINTS THE SAME MAN BOTH WAYS. All four of: the folded card's whole printed forename is a DISTINCTIVE WORD — not an initial, and not a given name the corpus uses as one — that no bearer in the cluster carries as a forename; exactly one documented bearer of the surname carries that word as a MIDDLE NAME PRINTED IN FULL, so the fold is onto a name the town has actually read rather than onto an expansion this rule supplies; a source OUTSIDE the two cards prints that one man BOTH ways — with his forename, and with the middle name standing alone in the forename's place — so the loss the fold supposes is one a page demonstrates; and no source prints the two readings as separate entries, which is D3's discriminator and the thing that would make them two men. Written for T-0993's Blanchard row. It is C6's shape with the initial replaced by a word, and it leans on a different leg: C6's fourth condition is an extraction flagged uncertain, because an initial is one of twenty-six and needs the doubt; a distinctive middle name needs instead that some source be caught printing the man both ways, and that is what this rule asks for in its place. Drop any one of the four and the card stays where it is.
rules.C9: ONE SURNAME, TWO SPELLINGS OF ITS ENDING, DEMONSTRATED IN ONE COLUMN. C7's shape for a surname whose variation is not a Dutch or French particle but a letter of the name itself. All four of: the forename and the middle initial agree on every printing, so nothing but the spelling of the surname stands between the cards; the SAME publication is caught setting both spellings for that one man inside the window — on one page, and better on one page-run — so the variation is the printer's and is demonstrated rather than supposed; the whole corpus holds exactly ONE bearer of that forename-and-middle-initial at this town, and no source places two such people here at once; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. The demonstration is the load-bearing clause, exactly as it is in C7: a merge across two printed surnames needs the printer's own inconsistency in evidence, not a reader's willingness to believe in it. A ONE-LETTER RESEMBLANCE IS NEVER ENOUGH ON ITS OWN, and T-1001 measured what it would cost if it were: turned into a mechanical fold over the land register's 427 named purchaser spellings, admitting one letter gathers a new rival for 200 of them and changes the shape of 42 proposals, 18 of which are already ruled by hand — tools/measure_surname_fold.py prints the table. That is why this rule asks for a page and not for a resemblance, and why it is applied one cluster at a time.
rules.C10: ONE FORENAME, TWO SPELLINGS OF IT, DEMONSTRATED IN ONE TITLE. C9's shape moved from the surname to the forename, and drawn to the same four conditions. All four of: the SURNAME agrees letter for letter and every middle initial agrees on every printing, so nothing but the spelling of the forename stands between the cards; the SAME publication is caught setting both spellings for that one man inside the window, so the variation is the printer's and is demonstrated rather than supposed; the whole corpus holds exactly ONE bearer of that surname-and-middle-initial at this town, and no source places two such people here at once; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. The demonstration is the load-bearing clause, exactly as it is in C7 and C9 — a merge across two printed forenames needs the printer's own inconsistency in evidence, not a reader's willingness to believe in it. Written for T-1002's Heacock row. A ONE-LETTER RESEMBLANCE IS NEVER ENOUGH ON ITS OWN and this rule is not a licence to fold on distance: tools/measure_card_fuzzy_candidates.py puts one letter of slack over the town's own cards and it proposes 71 pairs the exact test does not, among them John Hale against John Vale, Mark Noble against Mary Noble and James Sheldon against James Wheldon. A distance cannot tell those from this one. That is why the rule asks for a page, and why it is applied one cluster at a time.
rules.C11: TWO SPELLINGS DISCHARGING ONE DOCUMENTED OFFICE, WITH A NON-NAME DISCRIMINATOR. The shape C10 cannot reach: two spellings of one forename that NO single title is caught setting both ways, where the printings are nevertheless tied together by an office the town's own record holds. All four of: the surname agrees letter for letter and the middle initial or middle name agrees, so nothing but the forename's spelling separates the cards; BOTH spellings are printed in the discharge of ONE seat that only one person can hold at a time, so a second bearer is not merely unattested but impossible against the record; an INDEPENDENT NON-NAME DISCRIMINATOR ties the two printings to that one seat — a vote tally, a term of office, a signature on an instrument — and not the name, which is the thing in dispute; and the folded card carries no fact the survivor's record contradicts. Written for T-1002's Beaubien row, where the discriminator is an election return: two histories print the same five names and the same five vote tallies for the town's first board of trustees and spell the third man's forename two ways, and the town's own ordinance then names four of those five, under the second spelling, as the committee the board appointed. THE OFFICE IS THE LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE and it is narrower than a trade or an address: a trade two men can share and a street two men can live on, so neither would satisfy this rule. Drop any one of the four conditions and the card stays where it is.
rules.C12: ONE ALPHABETICAL RUN THAT NAMES EVERY BEARER, AND SETS ONE OF THEM UNDER THE DISPUTED SPELLING. The shape neither C10 nor C11 can reach: two spellings of one forename that NO single title is caught setting both ways, so C10's demonstration does not exist, and which NO ONE SEAT holds, so C11's office is not in evidence. What stands in their place is a printing of a different kind — a directory or a roster that sets out EVERY bearer of the surname at this town in one alphabetical run, so the page has undertaken the whole question and its answer is legible in what it does NOT print as well as in what it does. All four of: the SURNAME agrees letter for letter and the middle initial or middle name AGREES on the disputed printing, so nothing but the forename's spelling stands between the cards; that printing carries at least one NON-NAME attribute — a trade, an address, an office — which the survivor's record already holds from a source OUTSIDE it, so the identification is carried by the man's life and not by his name, which is the thing in dispute; the SAME RUN enumerates the surname's other bearers at this town, each under a forename that neither spelling can be read as, and prints NO entry under the survivor's own usual spelling, so the rivals are excluded ON THE PAGE and the disputed entry is standing where the survivor's entry would otherwise be; and no source is caught printing the two spellings as SEPARATE ENTRIES, which is D3's discriminator and the thing that would make them two men. THE ENUMERATION IS THE LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE, and it is what a directory can give that a history cannot: a history names whom it chooses and its silence means nothing, while an alphabetical run is a page that set out to name them all, so a spelling absent from it is absent because the compositor set the other one. Written for T-1026's Beaubien row, where C10's title and C11's seat both fail and Fergus's directory of 1839 prints the town's four Beaubiens in four consecutive lines. A RESEMBLANCE IS STILL NEVER ENOUGH: this rule is not reached by measuring a distance between two forenames — tools/measure_card_fuzzy_candidates.py prices that and T-1002 refused it — it is reached by a page that enumerates. Drop any one of the four conditions and the card stays where it is.

rulings.for: The owner's own demonstration in T-0839. Four cards, one man: Lieut. James Allen of the United States Army, the harbour engineer. hh_allen_lieut_james is the only card that knows his trade (army_officer, from the Democrat of 13 August 1834, column 2) and the only one the ladder never reached; hh_allen_james is the one the ladder graded best and it knows nothing about the army. 'Lieut Allen', 'Lieut J Allen' and 'Lieut. James Allen' are the same title, the same initial and the same full name, printed by the Democrat and the American between March 1834 and July 1835; 'James Allen' is that full name without the rank. Merged he is one attested man with a trade, four sources and two newspapers behind him.
rulings.against: Nothing reached says the town held a second James Allen. Two other Allens are on cards and both are ruled distinct below on their own forenames.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the card that carries the TRADE, because the trade is the thing a merge onto any other card would lose: mint_civic_residents.py writes `occupation: none_recorded` onto every card it derives and would re-derive an army officer away.

rulings.against_merge: Edward Richards Allen and William Allen are full forenames, and neither is James. They are in this candidate cluster only because a title-only card — 'Lieut Allen' — is compatible with every Allen in the town, which is what R1 exists to say.
rulings.for_merge: Nothing but the surname.

rulings.for: The owner names Hubbard on six as the worst case in the ticket. Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard is the one Hubbard the town documents — a packer at the old bank building, in Andreas and on the 1833-1835 voter rolls — and 'G. S.', 'Gurdon S.' are his initials, 'Gordon S.' is his forename mis-set, and 'G. T.' is the same initials with the S read as a T off a manuscript poll list. The Democrat, the American, the 1840 census, Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 are spread across the five.
rulings.against: T-0855. THIS RULING ONCE FOLDED A SIXTH CARD, 'hubbard_g', AND THAT WAS WRONG. Its earlier reasoning read 'No second Hubbard household is on any card, and no source reached names one', and both halves are false: hubbard_henry_g is a second Hubbard on a card in this same tree, attested, and hubbard_g's own and only press evidence reads 'Hubbard, [Henry] G.' citing person_hubbard_henry_g. A bare 'G.' has TWO rivals here — Gurdon and Henry G. — which is the case C2 refuses on principle. hubbard_g is now ruled onto Henry under C5, below. The five cards left here are not in question: none of them reads as anything but Gurdon.
rulings.survivor_note: hubbard_gurdon is hand-authored from Andreas and carries the trade, the arrival of 1818 and the premises; no derivation pass owns it, so the union written onto it stays.

rulings.for: hubbard_g's only press evidence is transcribed 'Hubbard, [Henry] G.' and cites record_id person_hubbard_henry_g. The bracket is the transcriber's own expansion, carried identically in five committed source files — fergus_1839_crosswalk_1835.json, fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json, newspapers/extracted/chicago_democrat_1835_08_05.json, newspapers/gazetteer.json and newspapers/register_1835.json — so it is a reading somebody made of the page rather than an inference from the initial. hubbard_henry_g is 'Henry G Hubbard', graded attested, already standing in the town.
rulings.against: 'G.' alone is also Gurdon's initial, and Gurdon is by far the better documented Hubbard — which is exactly why the initial cannot decide this and the transcription must. Ruling it onto Gurdon on the strength of his documentation is what T-0839 did, and it put one man's record on another man.
rulings.survivor_note: hubbard_henry_g is minted civic, so --apply does not write the union onto it: the appearance reaches him through the identity master and the mint, which is the pass that owns his card.

rulings.for: Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien is the documented Beaubien of the south division — trader, at his own homestead, in Andreas and on the voter rolls. 'J. B. Beaubien' is his initials letter for letter. 'John B. Beaubien' is the English rendering the Chicago papers used for Jean Baptiste all through the 1830s, and the middle initial B agrees.
rulings.against: The Beaubien surname holds more than one man, which is why the two other cards in this candidate cluster are refused below rather than swept in.
rulings.survivor_note: Hand-authored from Andreas; no pass owns it.

rulings.against_merge: T-0839 names John S. Beaubien as a second man, not a duplicate of Jean Baptiste — the ticket's own worked warning. Josette LaFramboise Beaubien is Jean Baptiste's wife and is already a member of his household record; she is in this candidate cluster only because her forename begins with the letter J. and 'J. B. Beaubien' prints an initial.
rulings.for_merge: The surname, and in Josette's case one letter of a forename.

rulings.against_merge: Fergus 1843 prints them as two entries, one after the other: 458 `Brown, Rufus B., warehouse man, John P. Chapin & Co., res 189 Lake [died, Burlington, Wis., September 2, 1872, aged 69]` and 459 `Brown, Mrs. Rufus B., dress and cloak maker, 189 Lake, up stairs [died February 2, 1890, aged 73.]`. Two trades, two death notices eighteen years apart, one address — a husband and a wife at 189 Lake, and a directory does not enter one person twice under two spellings. The cards read as one person only because the splitter strips `Mrs` before it compares the names.
rulings.for_merge: Nothing but the strip. After it, both readings are `Rufus B Brown` letter for letter, which is M1 — and M1 firing here is the defect, not the argument.
rulings.survivor_note: Neither card moves. The derivation now holds them apart too: R6 in tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py refuses the merge and mints her a ladder rung of her own, so `Mrs Rufus Brown` stops being a card the ladder never reached.

rulings.for: John Harris Kinzie is documented in the north division — forwarding and commission, at his own store, Andreas and Waubun and the voter rolls. The middle initial is what carries this one: the Kinzie surname holds a James as well as a John, so the bare initial J would be two rivals and refused, but 'J. H.' agrees with John Harris and no card and no source reached reads James Kinzie with a middle initial at all.
rulings.against: James Kinzie is his half-brother and is on his own card. The initial alone would not have been enough.
rulings.survivor_note: Hand-authored; no pass owns it.

rulings.against_merge: T-0839's own warning: John H. Kinzie and James Kinzie are brothers, not a duplicate. Juliette Augusta Magill Kinzie is John Harris's wife and already a member of his household record.
rulings.for_merge: The surname, and the letter J.

rulings.for: THE CONTRADICTING MIDDLE INITIAL WAS NEVER PRINTED — IT IS A DIGIT. (T-0854, folded into T-0844 and ruled here.) chicago_democrat_1833_12_10#c012 transcribes the advertisement as 'TO LOAN, / JOHN 8. KINZIE, / [F]orwarding & Commission [MERCHANT] / CHICAGO—ILLINOIS', and the `as_printed` string the extraction records is 'JOHN 8. KINZIE'. `8` is a digit, and no compositor set a digit inside a personal name; the lines around it come off the same scan as 'WIBRORA TT' and '[uncertain: orwarding & Commission | Fi]', so the reading at this spot is demonstrably wrecked. 'John S. Kinzie' is the extractor's NORMALISATION of that digit and no witness supplies the S. This is the fourth instance of the digit-for-letter fault T-0721 holds — '8. G. Abbot', 'A. 8. Perry', 'James I1. Gabbs' — and the first that reached a card. WHAT IS LEFT ONCE THE S GOES is a card minted from one printing of 'John [unread]. Kinzie, forwarding and commission merchant, Chicago—Illinois'. Four Kinzie men stand on the town's cards — James, John H., Robert A. and this one — and John Harris Kinzie is the only bearer of the forename John. His own card's `works_at` is `jh_kinzie_forwarding_store`, from his own 1834 advertisement in the same paper: the trade printed beside the unread initial is his trade. That is C3, a bare forename onto an anchor, corroborated by the trade INDEPENDENTLY of the initials — the same corroboration T-0732 required, and cited, for the R. A. Kinzie merge in this cluster.
rulings.against: The Kinzie surname is the one T-0839 named as this project's trap, and T-0732 records a Kinzie mis-fold. The guard against repeating it is that nothing here rests on the surname: data/research/books/crosswalk.json's rule — nothing merged, linked or graded on a shared surname — governs, and this fold is made on the forename and the trade. The elder John Kinzie, dead in 1828, is held by no record in this project and is not a rival. T-0854 said the merge stayed the owner's call; T-0844 is the ticket that makes it, and tickets/README.md holds `blocked-owner` to rights, licensing, real money and what the project is — an initial nobody printed is not one of them.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the anchor: the north-division household with the forwarding store, Andreas, Wau-Bun and the voter rolls. T-0732 §Q1 predicted this line — 'Four Kinzie household cards now stand where the ticket counted six. The count could yet fall to three' — and it is three.

rulings.for: The owner names Owen on five. Thomas Jefferson Vance Owen — United States Indian agent, first president of the town's board of trustees, born 5 April 1801, died at Chicago 15 October 1835 (Andreas, scan p. 195) — is the one Owen the town documents, and 'T. J. V.', 'Th. J. V.' and 'Thomas J. V.' are his initials. The fourth card is the striking one: 'Thomas Owen' was minted from st_cyr_death_07_1, where he is the DECEDENT, and the register dates that death 1835-10-15 — the day Andreas gives for Owen's death, from an independent source in another domain. The merge turns a bare G2c church card into a second, contemporary attestation of a death this project had on one nineteenth-century compilation alone.
rulings.against: The scene date is 1 July 1835 and the death is fifteen weeks after it, so the register entry contradicts nothing on the surviving card. No second Thomas Owen is named anywhere reached.
rulings.survivor_note: Hand-authored from Andreas; no pass owns it.

rulings.for: Dr John Taylor Temple — physician, at the Temple building, Andreas and the Baptist history and the voter rolls — is the one Temple whose initials are J. T. The Democrat prints him as 'J. T. Temple'.
rulings.against: His brother Dr Peter Temple is in the same household, but his initial is P.
rulings.survivor_note: Hand-authored; no pass owns it.

rulings.against_merge: Dr Peter Temple is John Taylor Temple's brother and Mrs Temple is his wife; both are already members of his household record and both are named separately by Andreas.
rulings.for_merge: The surname, and the household.

rulings.for: C6, ON A SIGNATURE LINE THE EXTRACTION ITSELF COULD NOT READ. `temple_t` is minted from one claim, chicago_democrat_1834_12_03#c022, whose quote runs '[uncertain: inieied Store, on SouhOBN T: TEMPLI]' and whose normalisation reads 'Also, a large and beautifully [fi]nished Store, on South [Water street.] T. TEMPLE. Chicago, Sept. 20, 1834.' What is advertised is a three-storey store house sixty feet in one dimension with a wharf attached, a small dwelling house of two rooms, and a finished store on South Water Street — river-frontage property, let by whoever owned it. The four conditions: (1) 'T.' is a forename initial for no Temple this town holds — the cards carry Dr John Taylor Temple and his brother Dr Peter Temple, and the press corpus's only other Temple is a '[Lew]is Temple' conjectured out of a letter list and minted onto no card; (2) exactly one documented Temple carries T as a middle initial, John Taylor Temple; (3) the same paper sets that man with both initials — 'J. T. Temple' eight times in this corpus and 'Dr. J. T. Temple' beside it — so 'J. T. TEMPLE' losing its first initial is a loss the source demonstrates rather than one this ruling supposes; (4) the printing is flagged uncertain by its own extraction. He is also the Temple the property records reach: he stands in the public-domain land tract sales, and three separate advertisements give his premises as the town's landmark at the corner of Lake and Franklin, one block off South Water.
rulings.against: A card whose only forename token is a MIDDLE initial has no rule in this project, and T-0839 refused to invent one because a loose rule would attach every stray middle initial in the corpus. C6 is written for that objection and states where it does not fire: drop any one of its four conditions and the card stays where it is. Dr Peter Temple is on the survivor's own household record and his initial is P, so he is not a rival for the T.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the anchor: physician, arrived early July 1833 with a wife and four children, Andreas and the Baptist history and the voter rolls and the land tract sales. `temple_t` carries one advertisement.

rulings.for: The owner names Fullerton on four. Alexander N. Fullerton — attorney, south division, Andreas and the voter rolls — is the one Fullerton the town documents; 'A. N.' and 'Alex N.' are his initials and his forename abbreviated, and 'Alexander M.' is the same name with the N read as an M off the poll list.
rulings.against: No second Fullerton is named anywhere reached.
rulings.survivor_note: Hand-authored; no pass owns it.

rulings.for: The owner names Haddock on four, and it is the case that fixes the shape of C4: E. / E. W. / Edward E. / Edward H., one documented Edward H. Haddock keeping the Mansion House in the south division, in Andreas, the Democrat, the 1840 census, the voter rolls and the Tribune's old-settler deaths. The middle initial is the only thing that varies and it varies across three manuscript and printed lists.
rulings.against: No second Haddock is named anywhere reached.
rulings.survivor_note: Hand-authored; no pass owns it.

rulings.for: The owner names Kimberly on four. Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly — physician, partner in the Pruyne & Kimberly drugstore, Andreas, the history of medicine in Chicago and the voter rolls — is the one Kimberly the town documents; 'E. S.' and 'Ed S.' are his initials, and 'Edmund L.' is the same forename with the S read as an L.
rulings.against: No second Kimberly is named anywhere reached.
rulings.survivor_note: Hand-authored, and a PARTNER in hh_pruyne_kimberly rather than a head — the merge lands on the person, not the household, and Peter Pruyne's record is untouched.

rulings.against_merge: John and Josiah are two full forenames, and the project's ratified rule has never merged one full forename onto another.
rulings.for_merge: Both are in Fergus 1843 and Norris 1844 as well as the town's own lists, which is a shared corpus and not a shared identity.
'J. B. Cook', a documented baker from the Democrat of 5 November 1834, shares a surname with both.
rulings.against_merge: The initial J has two rivals in this cluster — John and Josiah — and R2 refuses both. Josiah's middle initial P contradicts B outright; John's is unrecorded, so nothing decides. Refused by a ratified rule rather than referred: the next pass will refuse it identically and needs no ballot.

rulings.for: John S. C. Hogan — postmaster, at his own store in the south division, Andreas and the voter rolls — and 'J. S. C. Hogan' in the American and the Democrat are the same three initials in the same order.

THE PROOF HERE IS NOT BROWN'S PROOF, and the difference is why this ruling is written out rather than cited: R6 and D3 were built on ONE SOURCE PRINTING BOTH READINGS as separate entries, because `Mrs. Rufus B. Brown` and `Brown, Rufus B.` are identical once the honorific is stripped and nothing in the letters tells a Rufus from an Eliza. These two are not identical after the strip — `Taylor, C.` against `Taylor, Charles H.` — so the pair never needed that proof to be held apart; what joins them is the ordinary initial rule (C2 on the card side, M2 in the derivation) reaching across an honorific it cannot see. That is an argument for a KINSHIP, not for one card: R6 (#998) settled that a wife is not her husband.

rulings.for: THE PAGE THE TICKET ASKED FOR, READ — and it answers more than it was asked. The Chicago Democrat of 4 February 1834 (page 3, column 2, transcription lines 2092-2148) prints the officers the Chicago Temperance Society chose at its annual meeting in the Presbyterian Church on Thursday 30 January 1834, and its executive committee reads '[M]r. H. Vax Den Bocart' — normalized by the reading pass as H. Van Den Bogart. That is the printing this ruling was owed. THREE THINGS CAME WITH IT. (1) THE SAME PAPER SETS THE PARTICLE THREE WAYS. Searching the whole deposited Democrat run for the stem finds a THIRD Chicago printing nobody had extracted: the issue of 29 October 1834 (page 2, column 2, transcription line 970) carries 'H. Ven De Bogart' in the committee of seventy the anti-gambling town meeting appointed under J. H. Kinzie, standing among Whittier, Mosely, Fullerton, Beaubien, Saxton, Clybourn, Aaron Russell and J. S. Wright. So within sixteen months the Chicago Democrat sets this one man's particle as 'Van Den', 'Ven De' and — in the letter list of 20 May 1835 — 'Vanderbogart'. The DEN/DER difference the undecided ruling turned on is a difference the printer himself does not hold to, and it cannot be asked to separate two men. (2) THE STEM HAS ONE BEARER HERE. The newspapers' gazetteer carries exactly two Bogart-stem persons, person_h_van_den_bogart and person_h_vanderbogart, and both are forename initial H.; the only other occurrence of the stem in the whole 1833-1835 corpus is JAMES BOGERT, Jr., a director of an Oswego, New York vessel-insurance company printed in the Democrat's advertising columns of 17 June 1835, who is not a resident and is not an H. (3) THE HONORIFIC IS NOT DECIDED AGAINST THE DOCTOR. The column's left edge is clipped by one to four characters on almost every line of that notice ('[Ann]ual Mee[t]ing', '[C]apt. D. Wilcox', '[Li]eut. J. L. Thompson', '[Mr]. D. Harmon'), and the Bogart line survives as 'r.' with exactly one character lost — which 'Dr.' fits as exactly as the 'Mr.' the transcriber supplied. The two physicians on the same list, Dr John T. Temple as president and Dr Josiah C. Goodhue as vice-president, keep their 'Dr.' because their lines were not clipped. This is NOT read as an attestation that the committee man was a doctor; it is the narrower and sufficient point that the printing does not say he was not, so the honorific cannot be held against the fold. AND THE DATES BRACKET RATHER THAN CONTRADICT. Fergus's old-settler death notices print Dr Henry Van der Bogart twice (fdn0049, fdn0683) as dying at Naperville, Illinois on 8 April 1835; the letter 'Vanderbogart, H.' was advertised uncalled-for at the Chicago post office on 20 May 1835. A letter that goes uncalled-for six weeks after the man it was addressed to died is what these lists are for, and the deferral's own worry — recorded when this cluster was sent to T-0950 — resolves in favour of the fold rather than against it.
rulings.against: The particle is the whole of it, and it is now answered by the printer's own practice rather than by resemblance. What remains genuinely unproved is narrower and is stated here rather than buried: no single source prints two of these three readings side by side, so the fold rests on the corpus holding one bearer of the stem and not on one page naming the same man twice. Were a second H. Bogart of any particle to be read at Chicago in this window, this ruling is the thing to reopen.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is vanderbogart_henry, the only card that carries the FULL forename and the death notices behind it. The two folded cards each carry one press appearance and an initial: vanderbogart_h is the letter-list mint of the 20 May 1835 return, which vanderbogart_henry already cites at the same locator (chicago_democrat_1835_05_20#c013, record person_h_vanderbogart) — the plainest duplicate in the cluster, two cards on one printed line — and vandenbogart_h is the 4 February 1834 Temperance notice, which no other card holds and which the survivor gains by the fold.

clusters.why_not_derived: THE CANDIDATE TEST CANNOT SEE THIS PAIR, AND THAT IS THE FINDING UNDER IT. `compatible()` weighs the FIRST forename token of each card — a full word against the same word, or an initial the word begins with — so `gantry` against `f gantry` is two different words and the two cards never fall into one bucket. Every duplicate this project has folded so far was one the derivation raised; this one was found by hand, by T-0990 reading the land register, and it is written into this file as a cluster of its own so the ruling is read by the same machinery. Widening `compatible()` to reach it is NOT done here: a rule that matches any forename token against any other would put every man's middle name in a bucket with every other man's first, and the cluster list is a worklist somebody has to read.

rulings.for: C7, AND THE TOWN'S OWN DIRECTORY PRINTS THE NAME WHOLE. Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells [died, Brooklyn, N.Y., 1872.]' — forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey — and Fergus 1839 and Norris 1844 print the same man 'Francis G.' So the token the town carries as `Gantry` is that middle name, and the two cards are one word apart. The four conditions: (1) `Gantry` is a whole word and no Blanchard in the cluster carries it as a forename — the layer holds F Gantry Blanchard, W. G. Blanchard and, in the directories only, Joseph Blanchard the blacksmith; (2) exactly one documented bearer carries `Gantry` as a middle name printed in full, `blanchard_f_gantry`, whom the poll of 1834 prints 'Blanchard, F. Gantry' and Fergus 1843 prints out in full — W. G. Blanchard carries only the INITIAL G and never the word, so he is not a second bearer of it; (3) a source outside both cards prints this one man both ways, at one sale, in one week: the Illinois State Archives' public-domain land tract register enters the school section — section 16, T39N R14E, type SC — as 'BLANCHARD F G' and 'BLANCHARD F G AS' on 22 October 1833 (purchase nos 0376893-0376895, volume 818 page 010) and as 'BLANCHARD GURTREY' on 22 and 24 October 1833 (purchase nos 0367525-0367530, volume 817 page 027). A clerk dropping the forename and setting this man's middle name alone is therefore a thing the record does, not a thing this ruling supposes; (4) no source prints the two readings as separate entries. The two cards stand on two different lists of one volume — tax_1833 entry 5 'Blanchard, Gantry', poll_1834 entry 13 'Blanchard, F. Gantry' — and each list holds exactly ONE Blanchard. D3's discriminator is a source printing both, and no source does. WHAT THE MERGE GAINS: the arrival bound moves from 1834-12-31 back to 1833-12-31 on the tax list's own evidence, and the town stops holding a `projected_resident` who is in fact its best-documented Blanchard.
rulings.against: The two readings are genuinely separate readings and not one extraction read twice — different lists, different years, different lines of data/research/civic/records/voter_lists_1833_1835.json — so the case is not the easy one where a duplicate is a transcription artefact. Against that: a tax list of 1833 and a poll list of 1834 are exactly the pair a man appears on twice, and appearing on both is the ordinary case, not the suspicious one. The one thing that would say two men is a father and a son sharing the surname, one printed Gantry and one F. Gantry; nothing reached prints a second Gurtrey Blanchard anywhere — not the directories of 1839, 1843 or 1844, not the press corpus, not the church registers, not the land register, whose four spellings of the surname are all readings of this one name. W. G. Blanchard is the layer's other documented Blanchard and his forename initial is W, which is not F and is not Gantry; he stands, and is ruled distinct below.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is the card the DIRECTORIES reach. `blanchard_f_gantry` carries five sources, the 1839 and 1844 later-trade and later-address blocks, and the land register's rows; `blanchard_gantry` carries one line of the tax list of 1833. Both are civic mints, so the fold lands through the crosswalk and mint_civic_residents.py re-spends the joined identity — nothing here is written onto the card by hand.

rulings.against_merge: W. G. Blanchard is a house-and-land agent the Chicago Democrat names on 9 July 1834, and his forename initial is W. Francis Gurtrey Blanchard's is F. rulings.for: ONE NEWSPAPER SETS THIS MAN'S FORENAME BOTH WAYS INSIDE THE WINDOW, AND THE CARD THAT CARRIES THE SECOND SPELLING RESTS ON A WRECKED SCAN. (1) THE DEMONSTRATION. The Chicago Democrat prints him 'Russel E. Heacock,' — one l, a clean reading — in the county election return of 13 August 1834, issue page 2 column 5, lines 1966-2037 (claim c005 of data/research/newspapers/extracted/chicago_democrat_1834_08_13.json), where he stands as a candidate for Sheriff; and 'RUSSELL FE. HEACOCK' — two l's — at the head of his own law advertisement of 29 July 1835, issue page 3 column 6, line 442 (claim c018). One title, two spellings, eleven months, the same attorney, and in his own advertisement both times over. (2) AND THE FOLDED CARD'S OWN READING IS NEITHER. `heacock_russell_e` is minted from chicago_democrat_1835_05_27#c007, the first appearance of that same advertisement, and what the scan prints at its head is 'RUSSEN L E. HEACOCK' — an L adrift from a garbled RUSSELL or RUSSEL, normalized to 'Russell E. Heacock' by the extraction. So the doubled l on that card is the transcription's reading of a wreck, not a spelling anybody has read off the page; the printing it comes from is flagged `transcription_mediated`, and c007 and c018 are the same advertisement, dated 'Chicago, May 23, 1835' in its own last line. (3) THE SURNAME AGREES LETTER FOR LETTER AND SO DOES THE MIDDLE INITIAL. Nothing but the forename's second l stands between the two cards. (4) ONE BEARER, AND THE SINGLE l IS THE DOMINANT PRINTING BY EVERY OTHER BODY OF RECORD. Moses and Kirkland volume 1 print 'Russel E. Heacock' six times and never otherwise — the one vote against incorporation (line 12324), the judges of the election of 1830 (11584), the licence to keep a tavern at his residence (11731), the county commission (12014), the settlers table's 'Heacock, Russel E' with year 1827 (10813) and the index (129251). The Fergus directory of 1843 prints 'Heacock, Russel'; the Illinois State Archives' land tract register enters HEACOCK RUSSEL; Andreas, on whom the survivor rests, prints 'Russel E. Heacock, who had come in 1827'. The town holds no third Heacock card and no source reached names a second Russel(l) E. Heacock at this town. WHAT THE MERGE GAINS, AND IT IS THE LARGEST GAIN OF THE THREE: the land register's two Heacock purchaser spellings, HEACOCK RUSSEL E and HEACOCK RUSSELL E, are both REFUSED today under R2 — 'the forename names 2 of the 2 people of this surname, and a reading is named onto exactly one or onto none' — and the two rivals it cannot choose between are these two cards. With one card standing, each reading names one man and both refusals become matches: the register's crosswalk goes from 91 matched and 340 refused of 431 purchaser spellings to 93 and 338, measured by re-running tools/read_land_sales.py --build across this merge. A duplicate was not merely cluttering the count; it was withholding evidence from the man it duplicated.
rulings.against: THE TWO CARDS ARE MINTED FROM GENUINELY DIFFERENT READINGS — the survivor hand-authored off Andreas, the folded card off the Democrat of 27 May 1835 — so this is not the easy case where a duplicate is one extraction read twice. Against that: an advertisement a lawyer paid to have set week after week is exactly where a compositor's spelling wanders, and this one is caught wandering across its own reprints. THE THING THAT WOULD SAY TWO MEN is a son or a brother of the same forename and middle initial. Nothing reached prints one: Andreas counts the household as a wife and at least five sons and names NONE of them, which is why hh_heacock_russel_e carries one placeholder member and not seven invented people, and a son of 1835 old enough to advertise as a counsellor at law and to stand for Sheriff in 1834 would contradict the same source's 'his fifth son and youngest child was born' in the spring of 1835. NOTHING IS PROMOTED. The survivor's grade is attested before and after; the folded card's not_later_than bound of 27 May 1835 is later than the survivor's attested arrival of 1827 and moves nothing; the advertisement's own placement claim — a second-storey office opposite the corner of Lake and Franklin — is already carried where c007 put it and is NOT written onto the survivor's `works_at` by this merge, which would be a placement, and placement is T-0514's sequencing and not a card merge's business. THE SPELLING IS NOT TIDIED: the survivor stays 'Russel E. Heacock', which is what Andreas, Moses and Kirkland, Fergus 1843 and the land register all print.
rulings.survivor_note: The survivor is `heacock_russel_e`, HAND-AUTHORED, head of hh_heacock_russel_e, in the south division and in `heacock_house_monroe` — the house he built in the spring of 1835 and moved on rollers. The second member of that household, `heacock_household_unnamed`, is the wife and five sons Andreas counts and does not name; it is not a person, it is not touched, and it is not to be counted as one. The folded card is a civic mint standing `unplaced` with `present_on_scene_date: uncertain`, so the merge moves a man the town could not reach onto the card that houses him. Its sources and press evidence arrive on the survivor through the merge and through the card-merge crosswalk; data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json is DERIVED and re-derives from the merged layer, which is where the two refusals turn into matches.

also_ruled_on.what: The six clusters T-0839 referred to the owner, ruled. Four fold and two stand: Hunt and Kinzie because the contradicting middle initial turned out not to be printed at all, Kennicott because the anchor T-0839 said was missing is on its own card, Temple under the narrow C6; Saunders and Walker stand under D4. The town's cards fall by four. T-0854 is folded in here: the Kinzie reading is the first half of that cluster's ruling.

The Blanchard cluster, which the candidate test cannot derive and T-0990 found by hand while ruling the land register. `blanchard_gantry` folds onto `blanchard_f_gantry` under C7, a new rule written here for a MIDDLE NAME standing alone where a source is caught printing the same man both ways — C6's shape with the initial replaced by a word. W. G. Blanchard stands, distinct under D1. The town's cards fall by one.

THE TWO HUSBAND-NAME PRINTINGS R6 COULD NOT REACH, read on their own pages and ruled. HADLEY: a source DOES name her apart. Fergus 1843 prints `Hadley, Mrs. T. G. (Reed), dress and cloak maker, 147½ Lake` at e1164 and `Hadley, Timothy Gibson (Howard & H.), res alley bet N. Dearborn and Wolcott` at e1166 — two entries on one page-run, two trades, two addresses, and her own maiden name in the parenthesis the directory keeps for a firm. Norris 1844 repeats the pair at e0768 and e0769, the dress and cloak maker still at 147½ Lake. So she is her own identity, and what kept R6 off her was not the want of a page but the shape of the printing: her entry carries her husband's INITIALS and his carries his whole name, so the letter-for-letter test never looked. R6 is widened to the corpus's own initial rule, same source, one fit only — see tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py — and `id_hadley_timothy_gibson` gives her up. Neither Hadley is a resident of 1835: the town holds no Hadley card, and a directory of 1843 puts nobody in the town of July 1835. EGAN: no source names her apart, and none has to. `Mrs. Wm. B. Egan` is one line of the list of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office, the Chicago Democrat of 1 April 1834 (c001), and no body prints a bare `Wm. B. Egan` beside her, so R6 stands down and the widening above does not reach her either — `Wm` is an abbreviation, not an initial, and the same list is the only place the papers print the name. The ruling is that the line is HERS and not her husband's, and the town already holds her under her own forename: `egan_emeline`, Emeline Egan, wife, attested off Andreas, on the same card as Dr William Bradshaw Egan. So nothing is minted and nothing is merged; what is recorded is that a letter waiting for `Mrs. Wm. B. Egan` met the man's NAME and not the man — the same reading the Second Presbyterian roll's 34 husband-name lines already carry — and it is not evidence of Dr Egan's presence at the post office in April 1834.

THE KIMBERL(E)Y PAIR, AND THE FOLD THAT HID IT. `kimberley_ed` folds onto `kimberly_edmund_s` under C9, a new rule for a surname the printer sets two ways, written to C7's shape and leaning on the same load-bearing clause — a page that demonstrates the variation. The Chicago Democrat of 1 July 1835 sets both spellings in one column and 'Dr. Kimberly' four sentences after 'E. S. Kimberley' in one article. The town's cards fall by one. THE FOLD QUESTION THE TICKET ASKED IS ANSWERED WITH A COUNT AND THE ANSWER IS NO: tools/measure_surname_fold.py puts a one-letter fold over the land register's 427 named purchaser spellings and it gathers a new rival for 200 of them, changes the shape of 42 proposals — 24 named matches lost, 18 refusals turned into matches — and touches 39 of the 72 hand rulings, 18 of them by changing what the mechanical rule proposes underneath a written judgement. Among the casualties are PEARSONS HIRAM (against 'Hiram Pearson'), CLYBOURNE ARCHIBALD (against 'Archibald Clybourn'), LLOYD ALEXANDER (against 'Alexander Loyd') and PRUYNE PETER (against 'Peter Pryne') — every one of them the SAME man under a variant spelling, refused for having become his own rival — and T-0993's BLANCHARD GURTREY, whose hand `named` ruling the loose fold re-points onto the garbled card `blanshard_g`. So the mechanical fold stays exact and the variants are ruled here, one cluster at a time, on a page.

THREE DUPLICATE PAIRS THE CANDIDATE TEST COULD NOT SEE, BECAUSE EACH DIFFERS BY ONE LETTER — and the class they came out of, counted. All three fold and the town's cards fall by three. `beaubien_medore_b` onto `beaubien_madore` under C11, a new rule for two spellings discharging ONE DOCUMENTED OFFICE where no single title is caught setting both: the discriminator is the election return of 10 August 1833, whose five names and whose third tally — 23, the one distinctive number in it — Andreas and Moses and Kirkland print alike while spelling that third man's forename two ways and while disagreeing with each other about Owen's and Dole's votes, and the Democrat's own ordinance then naming four of those five, under the second spelling, as the committee the board appointed. `clybourn_archibald` onto `clybourne_archibald` under C9, on a page that sets the surname both ways four lines apart. `heacock_russell_e` onto `heacock_russel_e` under C10, a new rule that is C9's shape moved from the surname to the forename: the Chicago Democrat prints 'Russel E. Heacock' in August 1834 and 'RUSSELL FE. HEACOCK' in July 1835, and the folded card's own reading is the wrecked 'RUSSEN L E. HEACOCK' of the same advertisement's first insertion. THE HEACOCK MERGE PAYS FOR ITSELF IMMEDIATELY: the land register's HEACOCK RUSSEL E and HEACOCK RUSSELL E were both refused under R2 for having two rivals, and those two rivals were these two cards; the register's crosswalk goes from 91 matched to 93 of 431 purchaser spellings across this merge. AND THE CLASS IS COUNTED RATHER THAN GUESSED AT, which was the ticket's third acceptance clause. tools/measure_card_fuzzy_candidates.py runs the candidate test again with one letter of slack — on the surname, and on the forename where the surname is exact — and over 1,376 cards it proposes 71 pairs the exact test does not, 63 folding the surname and 8 the forename, 12 of them already ruled. Three was not all there were and 71 is not a worklist this ticket can rule: the list holds real spelling variations the sources demonstrate (Foot/Foote, Forsyth/Forsythe, Lloyd/Loyd, Pearson/Pearsons, Pruyne/Pryne), cards minted off garbles that R5 refuses and T-0695 reads (chark for Clark, tmple for Temple, smow for Snow, mgregor for McGregor), initials gathered across a folded surname where R2 does the work, and pairs that are simply two people one letter apart — John Hale against John Vale, Mark Noble against Mary Noble, James Sheldon against James Wheldon. A distance cannot tell the first kind from the last, which is the same answer T-1001 reached over the land register's 427 purchaser spellings. So the remaining 68 go to an EPIC under the queue's own filing rule, and `beaubien_medard` — three letters from Madore, outside this class, and the subject of a committed note that already calls it the same man — goes to its own ticket.

THE THIRD BEAUBIEN CARD, RULED ON A DIRECTORY PAGE AFTER THE PARISH REGISTERS CAME BACK EMPTY. `beaubien_medard` folds onto `beaubien_madore` under C12, a new rule for two spellings of one forename where C10's title and C11's seat both fail: what stands in their place is an ALPHABETICAL RUN that undertakes to name every bearer of the surname, so its silence is evidence. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints the town's Beaubiens in four consecutive lines on printed page 6 - Charles, John B., Mark, and "Beaubien, Medard B. , merchant, South Water street" - with no entry under Madore, and the merchant of South Water street is the survivor's own trade and his own shop at the south-west corner of South Water and Dearborn. The town's own polls print the two spellings in complementary distribution, Medard in the alphabetical run of 1833 and Madore in that of 1834, neither list holding both. THE REGISTERS THE TICKET SENT THIS PASS TO ARE SILENT and the finding is recorded rather than buried: St Mary's baptisms 1833-1835 and St Cyr's marriages and deaths reach nine Beaubiens and no Medard and no Madore, so the baptismal-forename argument T-1026 proposed is neither demonstrated nor refuted and this ruling does not rest on it. The civic claim c003's note, which has said since it was written that the two are one man under two spellings and that the merge is not made there, now names the ruling that makes it. The town's cards fall by one, to the card that carries the office, the trade and the house; the poll list of the very election that returned him arrives on it.
